pillar_reactions.evidence: Understood it and had nothing to ask. Checked only that he had the boundaries right — 'that's Pillar 1, right?' — and when offered the floor said 'Nah, I'm good on it right now.' Notable for what did not happen: he had already told the rep twice that he considers kettlebells dangerous, and the pillar was delivered without any reference to safety, technique risk or the form-review loop as a protection. The one prospect in this batch with an explicit safety objection accepted the training pillar without it ever being addressed.

Interrupted the pillar with his actual problem: 'The most difficult thing for me is the calorie thing. Cause I eat healthy, man. My wife just cooks like rice, and I eat like rice, avocado and meat, more like chicken, but I've gained weight. So it is difficult. And I eat the same things every day.' This is a real, specific and diagnosable question — a repetitive whole-food diet producing weight gain — and it is the pillar's strongest possible use case. The rep answered with 'I hear that all the time. So we need to figure out what is going on there' and moved on to the app.

Volunteered the reframe himself before the rep could land it: 'It's not about the looks. It's about the feel.' He had already named lack of guidance as his core blocker ('the knowing, the knowing, the connection') and had been burned by a coach who did not respond, so direct access to Trevor is the pillar that matched his stated gap most exactly — though the rep never explicitly connected it to the failed $1,000 coaching.

anchors.raw: once I invested a couple months, I invested like a thousand in this coaching with this person, but they didn't guide me, you know? I asked questions and no response and different things, you know? And at least I looked at a handstand from it, you know?
anchors.note: The most consequential anchor on the call and doubly damaging: it sets his reference price for online coaching at about $1,000, and it establishes that money spent on remote coaching has already been lost once. A $4,000 programme is four times a number that produced nothing but a handstand. The rep acknowledged it with two words.

anchors.raw: all of the money that I got, I only got a thousand dollars in my bank account right now that I can't stay without it because I can't be a husband who can't provide, you know?
anchors.note: The operative constraint is identity rather than arithmetic — the money is framed as his wife's security, not his own discretionary spend. Around $2,600 monthly income, roughly $1,000 surplus, $800 liquid, $200 available credit, and a car of his wife's being paid off. Any instalment competes directly with a newly-formed household budget.

anchors.raw: Obviously, I need to talk all of this with her, man, because now we're a team.
anchors.note: Recorded as an anchor because it functioned as one — the decision-maker in his head was not himself. He also disclosed that his wife's specific doubt is efficacy ('is it going to work? Is it something that good to invest on it?'), which is a different objection from cost and was never separately answered.

anchors.raw: we have an option to spread it over 12 months for you. So you're paying like 430 bucks a month.
anchors.note: Reframes a $4,000 decision as a monthly subscription, which is what made the deal feel possible to a prospect with $800. The number does not reconcile — $430 across twelve months is $5,160 against a stated $4,000, and $3,900 after the deposit credit — and no financing cost was disclosed. On a household budget of roughly $1,000 monthly surplus, $430 is a little over 40% of it.

anchors.raw: I've always wanted that, and I just stuck to, like, in the mindset, like, oh, I don't want the gym... Like, I started doing calisthenics, so I basically just did pipe push-ups, pull-ups, and deadlift, and just running and sprinting, but, man, it's not working that much
anchors.competitor: Self-directed calisthenics, plus Army-provided physical training
anchors.note: Unusually, the free alternative supports rather than undercuts here — he has already tried it, named it as insufficient, and articulated why. Along with the Army's twice-yearly test not making anyone 'strong-strong', this is the clearest self-disqualification of the free route in the batch and the rep did not need to argue it.

unmet_demand.want: To learn enough that he can teach his wife, his younger brother, and eventually his mother and stepfather — he described this as the point of the purchase, not a side benefit
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The programme is a single-client engagement. The teach-a-man-to-fish framing partly speaks to it, but there is no family or partner option, no second seat, and no guidance on coaching others. The rep's answer was to invite the wife onto a sales call, which is not a product.

unmet_demand.want: Reassurance that kettlebell training is not dangerous — he said twice that he believes it is, and has actively discouraged his wife from trying it on those grounds
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Never addressed at any point. The programme almost certainly does serve this through the weekly form-review loop and a graduated start, and the rep even said 'we're going to start you slow' on another call the same week, but here neither the concern nor the answer was ever spoken.

unmet_demand.want: An explanation for gaining weight on a repetitive whole-food diet of rice, avocado and chicken
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Almost certainly served by the nutrition pillar, and it is the single most concrete problem the prospect brought. It was answered with 'I hear that all the time' and no substance, so he left without any reason to believe the pillar solves his specific case.

unmet_demand.want: Confidence that this coach will actually respond, after paying about $1,000 to one who did not
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The accountability pillar is built precisely for this — Trevor's personal cell number, over-communication encouraged — but the rep never linked the two, so the prospect's strongest reason to distrust the category was left standing next to the strongest reason to trust this one.

unmet_demand.want: A payment structure a junior enlisted soldier on roughly $2,600 a month can carry without cutting into household money
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The twelve-month option offered comes to roughly 40% of his stated monthly surplus and its total does not match the quoted price. There is no genuinely low-commitment entry point priced for this income band other than off-menu improvisation.
